system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium entry into motor nerve terminals and decrease acetylcholine release. Repetitive activation can transiently increase calcium accumulation and improve strength.
vignette: An older adult with a long smoking history develops proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, and reduced deep-tendon reflexes. Strength improves transiently after repeated muscle activation. Chest imaging reveals a hilar mass consistent with small-cell lung carcinoma.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Myasthenia gravis is primarily a postsynaptic disorder and often features ocular/bulbar weakness with preserved sensation; facilitation, autonomic symptoms, and SCLC strongly favor LEMS.
Botulism can cause autonomic dysfunction and descending paralysis but has an acute toxic presentation rather than a chronic paraneoplastic proximal weakness with facilitation.
Polymyositis causes inflammatory proximal myopathy but does not explain hyporeflexia, autonomic symptoms, or facilitation with repeated activation.
ALS produces upper and lower motor-neuron findings rather than an autoimmune presynaptic neuromuscular-junction syndrome with autonomic dysfunction and exercise facilitation.
key_expl: LEMS is a presynaptic autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder. Antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium-dependent acetylcholine release. The classic pattern is proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, hyporeflexia, and facilitation with activity; a substantial proportion of cases are associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.
objective: Recognize Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome from proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, hyporeflexia, exercise facilitation, and small-cell lung carcinoma.
